questions.question: Why does Go usually return errors instead of throwing exceptions?
questions.title: Explicit errors versus exceptions
questions.direct_answer: Go normally returns errors as values so failure appears in function signatures and at each call site. The caller chooses how to handle or propagate it without automatic stack unwinding. `panic` and `recover` provide unwinding for exceptional invariant failures, but they are not the routine error mechanism.

interviewer_intent.testing: Go's error-handling design rather than memorized syntax.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Claiming returned errors cannot be ignored or that Go has no stack-unwinding mechanism at all.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Compare visibility, caller policy, and control flow without declaring one model universally superior.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Returned errors make failure visible in the function signature.
Callers choose policy explicitly at the call site.
Ordinary errors do not unwind the stack automatically.
Exceptions can centralize handling but make non-local control flow possible.
Go keeps panic and recover for exceptional conditions, not routine failures.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
Go normally represents failure as an ordinary return value. A signature such as `Open(name) (*File, error)` tells every reader that opening can fail, and the call site shows the decision made for that failure. Control remains local unless the caller explicitly returns the error upward.

Exception-based systems can transfer control to a handler several frames away. That can centralize policy, but a function's ordinary return type may not reveal every thrown path. Go favors visible checks and simple value flow, even though this means propagation code appears more often.

For example, a three-step import can parse, validate, and store a record. After each call, Go code can add the operation's context and stop immediately. A top-level handler then translates the final error once. Each layer's contribution is readable in sequence rather than implied by an exception table.

Returned errors can still be ignored deliberately, so the model does not magically guarantee correctness. Go also has `panic` and `recover`, which do unwind a goroutine's stack, but convention reserves them for broken invariants or controlled internal boundaries. I describe this as an explicit default with an exceptional escape mechanism, not as the complete absence of exceptions-like behavior.

sections.title: Compare where the failure path becomes visible
sections.content:
The main contrast is not whether both models can report rich failures—they can. It is where the alternate control path is declared and who activates it. A returned error becomes data at the immediate call; a thrown exception activates runtime unwinding until a matching handler is found.

This shapes code review. Go repeats small decisions near calls, while exception-oriented code often concentrates decisions at broader boundaries. Good design in either model still needs clear ownership, useful context, and stable categories.

sections.title: Returned errors and thrown exceptions
sections.content:
| Dimension | Go error return | Thrown exception |
|---|---|---|
| Visible in ordinary signature | Yes | Depends on language and declaration |
| Transfer of control | Explicit branch or return | Automatic stack search |
| Local caller choice | Shown at call site | May be deferred to distant handler |
| Go mechanism for invariant failure | `panic` and `recover` | Usually same exception mechanism |

questions.question: What does the phrase errors are values mean in Go?
questions.title: Errors are programmable values
questions.direct_answer: The phrase means an error is ordinary data that can be returned, stored, wrapped, compared, typed, accumulated, or transformed. Code is not limited to repeating `if err != nil`; APIs can shape error values around the operation, provided every exposed failure is still checked and handled deliberately.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding errors as data and applying that model beyond rote nil checks.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Interpreting the phrase as permission to ignore errors or as a claim that every line needs a check.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Use a buffered writer or scanner-style API to show error state stored across operations.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: An error is a value implementing `Error() string`.
It can be stored, wrapped, classified, and passed between layers.
APIs can delay reporting while retaining the first failure.
Programming with errors can reduce repeated checks without hiding them.
Every exposed error still needs a deliberate final check.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
'Errors are values' means the language does not give error values a magical representation. An error is an interface value, so programs can return it, store it in a struct, pass it to another function, wrap it with context, classify it by identity or type, and combine it with normal control structures.

This matters because good Go code does more than repeat a nil check mechanically. An API can retain the first failure while a sequence of operations continues through one helper, then expose that stored error once at a meaningful boundary. `bufio.Writer`, for example, lets callers perform writes and reports buffered output failure when they flush.

For example, a small collector can ignore later writes after its first error, keeping call sites focused on the sequence being built. The caller checks `Err()` at the end and still receives the original failure. Error checking has been organized around the operation rather than removed.

The boundary is correctness: an API must document when failure becomes observable and whether partial progress matters. Deferring a check is unsafe if the caller needs to react between steps. I use error values to model the real workflow—classification, accumulation, or translation—while ensuring that the final owner always observes and acts on the error.

sections.title: Move the check to the natural operation boundary
sections.content:
Repetitive checks sometimes indicate that several calls form one logical transaction. A helper can retain the first failure, skip dependent work, and report once when the transaction ends. The state remains explicit inside a value rather than disappearing into global control flow.

This pattern has a cost: it may hide how far processing advanced. Use it only when the operation is all-or-nothing or when partial progress is separately recorded. Fine-grained handling remains necessary when each step has a different recovery policy.

sections.title: Store the first error across one operation
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  A[Write first part] --> B{stored error?}
  B -- No --> C[Write second part]
  B -- Yes --> E[Skip dependent writes]
  C --> D{write failed?}
  D -- Yes --> F[Store first error]
  D -- No --> G[Continue]
  F --> H[Final Err check]
  G --> H
  E --> H
```

questions.question: How do sentinel errors, custom error types, and predicate functions differ?
questions.title: Three ways to classify errors
questions.direct_answer: A sentinel exposes one stable error value checked with `errors.Is`; a custom type exposes structured details checked with `errors.As`; a predicate function lets the package answer a classification question without exposing its representation. Choose based on what callers must know and how much compatibility the package should promise.

interviewer_intent.testing: Trade-offs among the main public error classification designs.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Choosing based on syntax instead of caller information and compatibility needs.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain how a predicate can hide representation and evolve independently.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Sentinel: shared identity for one category; inspect with `errors.Is`.
Custom type: category plus fields; inspect with `errors.As`.
Wrapping can preserve a sentinel or type while adding context.
Every exported classification becomes observable API behavior.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
A sentinel is one exported error value representing a category such as `ErrNotFound`. Callers use `errors.Is`, which also works when context wraps that value. It is compact and ideal when the useful answer is only yes or no.

A custom type represents a category with data. A `*ValidationError` might expose `Field` and `Rule`, and callers use `errors.As` to retrieve it through wrappers. This is appropriate when those fields drive presentation or recovery rather than merely making the log message longer.

A predicate function such as `IsTemporary(err)` keeps the representation behind package code. The package can recognize several private types or causes and change that logic later while preserving one public question. The cost is another API function and possibly less interoperability than standard `Is` and `As` conventions.

For example, a storage package could expose `ErrNotFound`, a typed `ConflictError` with a current version, and `IsRetryable` for several transient dependency failures. Each mechanism answers a different caller question. I select the narrowest promise that supports real handling, because exported sentinels, types, wrapping behavior, and predicates all become compatibility commitments.

sections.title: Expose the question, not the dependency
sections.content:
Classification is an abstraction surface. A sentinel says a stable category exists. A type says named details are stable. A predicate says only the package's answer to one question is stable, leaving its internal evidence private.

These mechanisms can coexist, but overlap should be intentional. If every dependency error escapes through wrapping, callers may couple to implementation details instead of the package's own domain vocabulary. Translation creates a smaller and more durable contract.

sections.title: Classification choices
sections.content:
| Mechanism | Public promise | Caller tool | Best fit |
|---|---|---|---|
| Sentinel | One value/category | `errors.Is` | Not found, closed, unsupported |
| Custom type | Type and documented fields | `errors.As` | Validation data, paths, versions |
| Predicate | Result of one package-owned question | Function call | Retryability across private causes |
